title: Sitharaman: India-US trade talks hit plateau as tariff pressure narrows room for deal
excerpt: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman told the Munich Leaders Meeting that India-US trade negotiations have reached a point where further give and take is "very, very difficult," as a new US law threatens up to 100% tariffs over Russian oil purchases.
body:
• Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on October 5 that India-US trade negotiations have reached a plateau, with further concessions "very, very difficult" for both sides — New Delhi's bluntest public admission yet that the interim deal has stalled.
  • The squeeze tightened last week: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said a deal is "not imminent" after meeting Piyush Goyal, and a new US law gives President Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying significant Russian oil — India among them.
  • Despite the standoff, Indian goods exports to the US keep climbing: $42.79 billion in April–August, up from $40.39 billion a year earlier, even as exporters face tariff uncertainty.
  • What this means for you: if you export to the US, the picture stays murky — most Indian goods already face an extra 10% Section 301 duty in effect since July 24, 2026, and some American buyers are trimming bulk orders while the talks drag on. Price contracts defensively and track the next technical round before locking in long-term rates.

New Delhi acknowledges the impasse

Trade deal talks between India and the United States have hit a plateau, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday, delivering the clearest official acknowledgement so far that negotiations on an interim agreement have run out of easy trade-offs. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting 2026 in New Delhi, she said the proposed pact had been "hard and very vigorously negotiated" and that the talks had reached a point "beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult." She added that negotiations were continuing, but her tone was unmistakably cautious.

https://x.com/MumbaichaDon/status/2107134756852994142

The remarks land days after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said a trade agreement was not imminent, following his meeting with Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers' gathering.

"The negotiations are still ongoing although we would like to believe both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister of India

Context & Background

New Delhi and Washington have been chasing a bilateral trade deal since February 2025, working under a framework for an interim agreement announced in February 2026. The talks were meant to resolve long-running irritants over tariffs, market access and non-tariff barriers.

The February framework had assumed an 18% US reciprocal tariff on Indian goods. That rate lost its footing after the US Supreme Court struck down the legal basis for the reciprocal duties, forcing both sides to rework the terms. Most Indian goods currently face an additional 10% duty under a Section 301 action that took effect July 24, 2026, with petroleum products, steel, autos, pharmaceuticals and some farm goods exempt.

Room for compromise narrowed further after President Trump signed a congressional bill giving him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying significant Russian oil, including India and China. India, the world's third-biggest oil importer, ranks among Moscow's largest buyers — purchases Washington says help Russia withstand Western sanctions. The move puts Prime Minister Narendra Modi in an energy-policy bind: cutting Russian oil imports could raise fuel prices or strain government finances, while keeping them risks crushing tariffs on exports to India's largest market.

Impact & Analysis

The numbers tell a story of resilience under pressure. Indian goods exports to the US rose to $42.79 billion in April–August from $40.39 billion a year earlier, and commerce ministry data showed merchandise exports to the US up 21.83% year on year in August alone. Exporters have kept selling even without a deal.

But the uncertainty has a cost. Reports have said some US buyers are reducing bulk orders and diversifying sourcing while the tariff picture stays unclear. Ajay Srivastava, founder of the New Delhi-based Global Trade Research Initiative and a former trade official, argues India should hold its ground: "India should stop giving away concessions while the US trade deal remains unfinished."

Sitharaman pushed back on what she called the "weaponizing" of tariffs, saying levies had moved beyond their role as a negotiating instrument.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, a stalled deal has practical edges. Textiles, gems and jewellery and engineering goods — the labour-intensive sectors that employ millions back home and stock shelves in US markets — stay exposed to tariff overhang. A signed interim agreement would likely lift that cloud and ease pressure on the rupee and on the remittance math that diaspora families watch closely. For now, Sitharaman's "plateau" is a signal to brace for a longer wait rather than count on quick relief.

What's Next

Technical discussions are expected to continue, though the timeline for an interim agreement remains uncertain. Sitharaman pointed to the recently concluded India-EU agreement, which she called "the mother of all deals" covering roughly two billion people and a quarter of global GDP, as proof that India will sign big pacts — on its own terms.
